nameStory: The Common Tern gets its straightforward name simply because it's the most widespread and frequently seen member of the tern family across much of the world. The word 'tern' comes from an old Scandinavian word meaning 'to turn,' referring to their graceful wheeling flight patterns over water. They're so numerous and familiar that early bird watchers used them as the standard by which all other terns were compared.
description: The Common Tern is an elegant seabird about the size of a small gull, with long, pointed wings and a deeply forked tail that gives it a swallow-like appearance in flight. During breeding season, adults sport a distinctive black cap on their heads, light gray wings and back, and a bright orange-red bill with a black tip. They're masterful fishers, diving headfirst into water with incredible precision to catch small fish. These graceful birds are summer visitors to New England's coasts and lakes.

idTips.label: Black Cap
idTips.description: In breeding season, look for the jet-black cap covering the entire top of the head from bill to nape, creating a striking contrast with the white cheeks and neck

idTips.label: Orange-Red Bill
idTips.description: The slender, pointed bill is bright orange-red with a distinct black tip, looking almost like it was dipped in ink

idTips.label: Forked Tail
idTips.description: The deeply forked tail streams behind them in flight like long ribbons, much more pronounced than a gull's squared-off tail

idTips.label: Plunge-Diving Behavior
idTips.description: Watch for their spectacular fishing technique - they hover briefly over water, then fold their wings and dive straight down with a splash

idTips.label: Orange-Red Legs
idTips.description: The legs match the bill color, appearing bright orange-red when visible on perched birds

idTips.label: Harsh Call
idTips.description: Their voice is a harsh, grating 'kree-arr' or 'kek-kek-kek' that carries well over water and nesting colonies

habitat: Common Terns favor open waters and shorelines throughout New England, nesting on sandy beaches, rocky islands, salt marshes, and even artificial platforms like floating rafts. They're equally at home along the Atlantic coast and on inland lakes and large rivers. Look for their colonies on flat, sparsely vegetated areas near water where they can easily take off and land.

seasonality.spring: Migrants arrive in late April to early May, with adults showing their full breeding plumage including the distinctive black cap and bright orange-red bill. This is when they establish nesting colonies and begin courtship displays.
seasonality.summer: Peak breeding season when they're most visible and vocal around nesting sites. Adults are in full breeding plumage and actively fishing to feed their young.
seasonality.fall: Adults begin losing their black caps by late summer, developing a partial white forehead. Young birds show more mottled, brownish plumage. Most migrate south by September.
seasonality.winter: Absent from New England, having migrated to warmer coastal waters from the southern United States through South America.

funFact: Common Terns can dive into water from heights of 30 feet or more, and their eyes actually change focus underwater - they have special muscles that squeeze their lens to maintain sharp vision both in air and while submerged!
confusionNotes: Arctic Terns look nearly identical but have an all-red bill (no black tip) and shorter orange-red legs. Forster's Terns have a more orange bill and different tail pattern. Memory trick: Common Terns have 'common courtesy' - they dip their bill tips in black ink to be polite!
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'common,' these birds have actually declined significantly in North America over recent decades due to habitat loss and disturbance at nesting sites. Their nesting colonies are particularly sensitive to human activity, so viewing them from a respectful distance is important for their conservation.
compareHints: Compared to other New England terns, Common Terns are the most likely to be seen inland on lakes and rivers, while Roseate Terns stick closer to saltwater and have longer, more deeply forked tails. Arctic Terns have shorter legs and completely red bills, while Forster's Terns have more orange bills and grayer wing tips.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Compared to Common Terns, Roseates are more delicate with longer, more elegant proportions and that distinctive pink breast wash.
Forster's Tern differs from Common Tern most obviously in winter with its black eye mask versus the Common's black cap extending to the eye.
Among New England's terns, Arctic Terns are distinguished from Common Terns by their solid red bills (no black tip) and more deeply forked tails.
